name: Starter: Afrikaans
about: Afrikaans word order in real, everyday sentences.

words.wees: to be (is: am, is, are; was: was, were)
words.gaan: to go (hoe gaan dit: how are you; gaan + verb: going to)
words.toe: to (after a place: winkel toe, to the store)
words.het: past-tense helper: have, has (with a participle)
words.se: 's (my pa se kar: my dad's car)
words.kry: to get (koud kry: to be cold)
words.om: part of om … te: to; in order to
words.fliek: the movies (fliek toe: to the movies)
words.al: already; for (al 'n jaar lank: for a year)
words.lank: long ('n jaar lank: for a year)
words.sien: to see (sien jou môre: see you tomorrow)

hoe-gaan-dit.about: The everyday how are you, literally how goes it; the answer is often Goed, dankie.

kry-koud.about: Afrikaans says you get cold (Ek kry koud) where English says you are cold.

sien-jou-more.about: An everyday goodbye when you'll meet again tomorrow.

verskoon-my.about: To get someone's attention or say sorry, to anyone.

concept.line: A present-tense verb has one form for every person.
A yes/no question puts the verb first (Praat jy Engels?
ek and jy are I and you as the subject, my and jou are me and you after a verb or a word like vir, and my and jou before a noun are my and your: Praat jy Engels?; Wag vir my!; Wat is jou naam?
die is the (for every noun, one or many), and 'n is a or an: die stasie, die skoene, 'n boek.
kan (can), wil (want) and moet (must, have to) take the main verb at the end, with no to: Ek wil iets soets eet; Nou moet ek gaan; Ons kan 'n taxi neem.

Before a noun some adjectives take -e (nuut: nuwe skoene) while others normally stay unchanged ('n klein woonstel, 'n groot kombuis); on their own, after is, they take none (Dit is koud); after iets, standard Afrikaans normally adds -s (iets soets), although some speakers leave it off (iets soet).
